newsitem.title: USA: PJM dispute may slow U.S. East Coast power futures.
newsitem.headline: PJM dispute may slow U.S. East Coast power futures.

text.p: A dispute over how to price power at the Pennsylvania-Jersey-Maryland (PJM) Interconnect pool, a hub for East Coast electricity trading, could kill its chances of becoming a delivery point for electricity futures.

The controversy among power marketers, the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), and the utilities that trade power in the PJM pool, centers on whether rules aimed at ensuring reliable power supplies might split the pool into a cluster of inefficient mini-markets, industry sources said.
"Some of the rules to wholesale transactions could be detrimental to the (PJM) market," said an industry source.

One plan, concerned about stabilizing the grid, calls for limiting how much power can be sent over the region's high-voltage lines during periods of high demand or whenever outages hit key power plants or transmission lines.
Opponents of the plan argue it would split the pool into small, isolated systems, raising the need for separate pricing formulas, or "locational marginal prices" within the pool.

These, in turn, would be reflect a web of delivery points during high-demand periods and confound efforts to identify or a standard price against which to hedge, a point that is essential to the development of a PJM futures contract.
"It's too complex. For example, when it would kick in? It became a major concern for us," said an industry source closely following the debate.
Seven of PJM's eight utilities support locational marginal prices.
The dissenting utility, PECO Energy Co, NYMEX and regional power marketers have formed an alliance to fight the plan.

The seven-utility group believes that as the power market moves toward open competition, electricity prices should reflect differences in the demand and costs at various delivery points within the PJM pool.
"The costs will vary from one facility to another depending on congestion and loading on the system," said Public Service Electric and Gas Co spokesman George Koodray.
"Liquidity will disappear in a locational marginal price world," said John Brodbeck, a PECO transmission specialist.

He said the pricing plan back by the utility alliance would relegate too much control to the pool which would be in charge of calculating about 1,500 sets of market-clearing prices per hour during periods of transmission constraint.
"It squelches bilateral trading because the pool would be the overriding market mechanism," he said. "We see the market as being bilateral dependent on the pool's buyers and sellers"

PJM has been touted as a prime area for a delivery point for NYMEX to tailor an East Coast power contract because of its active cash activity, diverse fuel generation mix, fair price indication for other East Coast bulk markets.
Last March, NYMEX launched the country's first electricity futures contracts with delivery at the California-Oregon Border and the Palo Verde switchyard near Phoenix, Arizona.

Until late 1996, NYMEX was close to choosing a PJM delivery point, likely the Peachbottom switchyard near Philadelphia, industry sources said. In November, the Federal Regulatory Energy Commission (FERC) rejected the restructure plans of all PJM members.
PJM participants submitted revised proposals earlier this month. FERC is expected to rule by early March on plans including the issue of locational marginal pricing.

If FERC rules in favor of locational marginal pricing, NYMEX will likely re-examine delivery points in the interstate transmission systems of Cinergy, Entergy. Southern Co, American Electric Power Co and Tennessee Valley Authority, industry sources said.
"We're still looking at which delivery point," said a NYMEX spokeswoman, adding the exchange hopes to launch an East Coast electricity contract in the second half of 1997.
